summary: Describes the MIME header Content-Duration for time-varying media like audio and video. It obsoletes RFC 2424.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines a small mail header that says how many seconds a recording lasts. It is like the running time printed on a video case, so a program can show the length without playing the file.

questions: how do you state the length of a voice message in email
subtitle: A one-line mail header that states how many seconds an audio or video attachment lasts.

tldr.problem: A voice message or video clip has a running time, but you cannot see that time without opening and decoding the content.
tldr.mechanism: The Content-Duration header carries the length in seconds as a single number with no unit tag, written as one to ten digits.
tldr.outcome: A mail reader can show the duration without opening the media, but the number is only the sender's claim and must not be used to work out the real data size.

today: RFC 3803 is a Draft Standard published in June 2004 that obsoletes RFC 2424. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Header Is For
sections.content:
Content that changes over time, such as a spoken voice message or a video clip, has a duration of its own. Many audio and video encodings store that duration or allow it to be worked out from the byte length, but it can still be handy to state it in a MIME header so it is available without touching the content.

This document defines the Content-Duration header for such content, typically audio/* or video/*. It obsoletes RFC 2424, and the only changes are editorial and boilerplate.
sections.plainLanguage: To find out how long a recording lasts, a program normally has to open and read the whole file. Putting the length in the message header avoids that.

sections.title: Syntax and Meaning
sections.content:
The value is a single number giving the time in seconds, with no unit tag. The formal rule is duration := "Content-Duration" ":" 1*10DIGIT, so the number has one to ten digits. The practical upper bound is 2147483647, which is 2 to the power 31 minus 1. An example is Content-Duration: 33, meaning 33 seconds.

The value should be exact, but the exact duration cannot be known without opening and playing the content. If an exact figure is needed, playing it is the method to use; this header just lets a sender place a value where it is easy to reach. How a receiver presents it, for example in the inbox headers or when the attachment is opened, is a local implementation matter.
sections.plainLanguage: The number is a plain count of seconds, such as 33. It is the sender's best answer, not a measured reading, so treat it as an estimate.

sections.title: Use in Voice Mail
sections.content: The header is a useful part of the Voice Profile for Internet Mail version 2 (VPIM), specified in RFC 3801. Every VPIM message MUST contain the audio/32KADPCM sub-type to carry the audio of a voice message. Showing the duration helps, for example, on a simple MIME or non-MIME desktop where opening the audio is awkward.
sections.plainLanguage: Voice mail systems use this header so a person can see how long a spoken message is before deciding to listen.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Putting the duration in a header outside the binary data may be a security issue in some environments, though likely not most, and in those cases it should not be recorded. The value in the header cannot be trusted to determine the exact size of the data. The exact length must be found by examining the data itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not rely on the label when it matters. Check the real recording instead.
